**PSR publishes binding direction on Confirmation of Payee requirements**

*Specific Direction 17 formalises the verification of payee obligations that UK payment firms must meet, moving the regime from expectation to enforceable rule.*

The Payment Systems Regulator (PSR) published Specific Direction 17 on October 22, setting out binding requirements for Confirmation of Payee across UK payment service providers. The direction gives the PSR a formal enforcement tool for a service that has, until now, operated under a patchwork of industry commitments and regulatory expectations.

Verification of payee gaps have been a persistent theme over the past year. IBAN errors still slip through existing checks, and the PSR's own study found that mandatory APP fraud reimbursement cut losses by £73 million, partly by incentivising better prevention. Formalising the direction strengthens the PSR's hand to act against firms whose checks remain inadequate, and creates a clearer compliance baseline for new entrants, including open banking providers increasingly active in payment initiation.

The direction sits alongside the delayed verification of payee requirements under the EU's instant payments regulation, where implementation timelines remain a point of contention. The UK is now ahead on the enforcement side, even as questions about the effectiveness of existing checks persist.

*Sources: [PSR publishes Specific Direction 17 (Confirmation of Payee)](https://www.regulationtomorrow.com/2026/10/psr-publishes-specific-direction-17-confirmation-of-payee/) — Global Regulation Tomorrow*

**Sweden's Riksbank presses parliament to begin e-krona preparations**

*The ECB's approaching digital euro pilot and dollar-denominated stablecoins are forcing Europe's most cashless nation to reopen a CBDC debate it shelved three years ago.*

Riksbank deputy governor Per Jansson said on October 22 that Sweden's near-total shift away from cash makes a digital krona harder to defer. A Riksbank survey earlier this year found only 5% of Swedes had used cash for their most recent purchase. Jansson told Reuters that if the krona is not available in a usable digital form, it may struggle to compete with more convenient cross-border payment instruments.

The Riksbank published a letter to parliament's finance committee on October 15 arguing that preparatory legislative work should begin now, even though Sweden has not decided whether to issue an e-krona. A 2023 government inquiry had concluded there was no urgent need for a CBDC, but the Riksbank now cites the ECB's planned digital euro pilot in late 2027 and possible issuance in 2029, along with the growth of dollar-pegged stablecoins, as developments that have changed the calculation. Jansson estimated that legislation and implementation would take at least five years.

The Riksbank also framed payment system resilience as part of Sweden's total-defence strategy. Amanda Sundstroem, senior macro strategist at SEB, said the ability to pay during an attack or infrastructure failure is among the most vulnerable aspects of Swedish society. For European payment providers, the Riksbank's shift illustrates a broader pattern: the digital euro is not only a euro area project but a catalyst forcing non-eurozone countries to define their own digital currency positions or risk ceding ground to foreign instruments.

*Sources: [Swedish central bank revives e-krona debate as digital euro, stablecoin threat grows](https://www.globalbankingandfinance.com/swedish-central-bank-revives-e-krona-debate-digital-euro/) — Reuters (via Global Banking and Finance Review)*

**Italy proposes instant payments project to connect Balkans with EU infrastructure**

*Euro instant payments rails would extend into the western Balkans under a new Italian proposal, using financial integration as a tool for EU enlargement policy.*

Italian foreign minister Antonio Tajani announced a project at a summit in Montenegro on October 22 to build instant payments infrastructure connecting western Balkan countries with the European payments network. The initiative frames payment system integration as part of the broader EU enlargement agenda for the region.

The proposal follows a pattern of extending EU payment rails beyond the eurozone's current borders. Iceland signed an agreement on June 24 to connect to TIPS, with implementation scheduled for 2028. Greece linked its domestic IRIS system to European instant payments in July, and Montenegro itself launched instant payments using SEPA standards the same month. The Italian project would go further by creating a structured programme across multiple Balkan states, rather than individual country-by-country connections.

The project signals potential new volume on SEPA instant rails and fresh demand for compliance and connectivity services among payment infrastructure providers and banks active in south-east Europe. It also extends the geopolitical dimension of European payment autonomy that the Bank of Finland and others have been articulating throughout 2026.

*Sources: [Balkan enlargement at the center of the summit in Montenegro: Tajani announces a project ...](https://www.agenzianova.com/en/news/balcani-allargamento-al-centro-del-vertice-in-montenegro-tajani-annuncia-un-progetto-sui-pagamenti-istantanei/) — Agenzianova*

**FCA chief Nikhil Rathi frames open finance transition in City of London speech**

*Rathi's remarks position the shift from open banking to open finance as part of the FCA's broader market integrity agenda, linking it to the regulator's digital-era priorities.*

The Financial Conduct Authority's chief executive, Nikhil Rathi, addressed the transition from open banking to open finance in a speech on market integrity in the digital age, delivered in the City of London on October 22. The remarks placed open finance alongside AI and digital market conduct as pillars of the FCA's forward agenda.

The speech follows a sequence of FCA interventions on open finance this year. The regulator published its open finance roadmap in April with a 2030 target, consulted in June on mortgage rule flexibility, and in October its taskforce mapped open finance use cases and identified infrastructure gaps. Rathi's public framing of the agenda in a high-profile City setting reinforces the signal that open finance is being treated as a regulatory programme, not an aspiration.

The available summary of the speech does not include detailed new policy commitments. The FCA's chief executive publicly linked open finance to market integrity, rather than treating it solely as a competition or innovation matter.

*Sources: [Market Integrity In A Digital Age - Speech By Nikhil Rathi, UK Financial Conduct Authority ...](https://mondovisione.com/media-and-resources/news/speech-by-nikhil-rathi-uk-financial-conduct-authority-chief-executive-market-i-20261022/) — Mondovisione*
